clue.text: Carried by Tommy — or carrying little Tom?

definitions.meaning: Tommy Atkins is the British private soldier, who humps his gear in a canvas sack
read literally, a sack holding a kit, a young cat, the little one of a tom

explanation.surface: A soldier's burden set against a sack with a kitten inside.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy is the stock name for a British soldier. The second reading splits the answer: a KIT is a young cat (a 'little Tom'), and a BAG carries it.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier's canvas sack holds his kit, the uniform and equipment he carries on the march, so both readings describe the same sack.

clue.text: It's all up with the vessel, saucy though it be

definitions.note: describes a sauce, an adjectival phrase for a noun

parts.note: a ketch is a two-masted sailing vessel
taken as written

explanation.surface: A doomed boat described with mock-solemn cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'saucy' looks like 'cheeky'; it means 'made of sauce', the tomato kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A tomato condiment is a sauce, so 'saucy' fits it literally.

clue.text: There's something electric in birdsong in plenitude

indicators.note: in places the charged particle inside the bird's warbling

parts.note: trills are a bird's warbling notes
an ion is an electrically charged particle

explanation.surface: A charge seems to run through abundant birdsong.
explanation.definitionFit: Numbers in the millions of millions suggest vast abundance.

parts.note: the missing word from Sonnet 104, the yellowing season that follows summer

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare's sonnet with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Sonnet 104 reads 'Three beauteous springs to yellow autumn turn'd': the missing word is the season of falling leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: The season of falling leaves follows summer, the yellowing time of year in Shakespeare's line.

parts.note: short cinema previews of coming films are named as if they follow behind, yet they are shown ahead of the feature

explanation.surface: A film critic muses on the odd way cinema previews turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: The paradox: these previews take their name from trailing behind, yet they are shown before the film they advertise.
explanation.definitionFit: Short advertising clips of a coming film, shown in cinemas, are called by this name.

definitions.meaning: King Claudius in Hamlet says 'O, my offence is ...', foul
a line of soldiers side by side

explanation.surface: A king's crime in a row.
explanation.walkthrough: Claudius in Hamlet confesses 'O, my offence is rank, it smells to heaven'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's king calls his crime foul-smelling; separately, a row of soldiers abreast is a line.

parts.note: lines on a map joining places where the compass deviation from true north is the same

explanation.surface: A paradox about lines that show change without change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variation' is the magnetic variation, the angle between magnetic and true north; these lines join points where it is equal.
explanation.definitionFit: Map lines of equal magnetic declination are so called, from Greek for equal angle.

clue.text: No longer in on the turn ? Just so

parts.note: ex means former, no longer
a turn is a performer's act in a variety show

explanation.surface: Someone no longer in on the act agrees: quite right.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes 'in on the act'; a 'turn' is a music-hall act.
explanation.definitionFit: Exact means precisely right, as 'just so' does.

definitions.text: No —— of farewell When I embark" (Tennyson)

parts.words: No —— of farewell When I embark" (Tennyson)
parts.note: the missing word from Crossing the Bar, the grief Tennyson asks to be spared at his death

explanation.surface: A line of Tennyson with one word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's Crossing the Bar: 'And may there be no sadness of farewell, When I embark'.
explanation.definitionFit: The sorrow of parting is the missing word, the grief Tennyson asks to be spared.

clue.text: Corrupts the Scotsman's own among Pussyfoots

indicators.note: among puts the Scottish word for 'own' in the middle of the teetotallers

parts.note: 'Pussyfoot' Johnson was a US prohibition campaigner, so pussyfoots are teetotallers, TTs
AIN is the Scots word for own

explanation.surface: A Scotsman's goods are spoilt while he lives among teetotal campaigners.
explanation.walkthrough: William 'Pussyfoot' Johnson campaigned for prohibition, so his followers are TTs (teetotallers); AIN goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To corrupt something is to spoil or contaminate it, the verb sense of a stain or blemish.

definitions.meaning: read as not towards, i.e. heading away rather than forward

explanation.surface: Turning back is held to be a bad omen.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading splits the answer into UN (not) and TOWARD, so moving away rather than forward; the question mark flags that split.
explanation.definitionFit: Untoward means unfavourable or unfortunate; split, it means 'not towards', hence going away.

clue.text: Does this stuff come only in new blues ?

definitions.text: Does this stuff come only in new blues

parts.words: Does this stuff come only in new blues
parts.note: a cotton-and-wool dress fabric named after a French city, whose namesake in Louisiana gave its name to a jazz and blues style

explanation.surface: A shopper asks if a fabric is sold only in new blue shades.
explanation.walkthrough: The fabric is named after the French city; 'new blues' points to the New Orleans blues of jazz.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloth of cotton warp and worsted weft took its name from the French city.

parts.note: an assay mark stamped on gold or silver attesting its quality, and by extension any mark of excellence

explanation.definitionFit: The stamp of the assay office on precious metal guarantees its purity, so it is a mark of quality.

clue.text: Bottom had "a great desire to a —— of hay"

definitions.text: Bottom had "a great desire to a —— of hay

parts.words: Bottom had "a great desire to a —— of hay
parts.note: the missing word from Bottom's line in A Midsummer Night's Dream, spoken when he wears an ass's head: a bundle of hay

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare with one word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: Bottom the weaver, given an ass's head in A Midsummer Night's Dream, says 'Methinks I have a great desire to a bottle of hay'. An old sense of the word is a bundle of hay or straw.
explanation.definitionFit: In old usage a bundle or truss of hay was called by this name, the word Shakespeare gives Bottom.

parts.note: in a duel, the insulted party demands satisfaction, settled by firing hand guns

explanation.surface: Releasing something brings contentment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'satisfaction' is the duellist's sense: amends for an insult, obtained by firing at each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Hand guns were the duellists' weapons, fired to settle a point of honour.

parts.note: an architectural support, reread as the stay of an aeroplane, a slang name for its ...

explanation.surface: An architect's term for the arched support of a cathedral wall.
explanation.walkthrough: A flying buttress is an arched support; 'flying' also points to an aircraft, whose propeller is called by the same short word.
explanation.definitionFit: A buttress is a support, and so is this word; it is also slang for an aircraft's propeller, the thing that flies.

parts.note: read not as talented folk but as those who have been given presents

explanation.surface: Talented individuals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gifted' looks like 'talented'; here it means 'given a gift'.
explanation.definitionFit: People who receive presents are those to whom something has been given.

clue.text: First sources of honey in a bee loud glade

definitions.text: First sources of honey in a bee loud glade

parts.words: First sources of honey in a bee loud glade
parts.note: the glands in flowers that secrete the sweet liquid bees collect, echoing Yeats's bee-loud glade

explanation.surface: Yeats's Innisfree, where bees hum among flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bee-loud glade' is from Yeats's The Lake Isle of Innisfree. 'First sources' looks like a first-letters signal; it means where honey begins.
explanation.definitionFit: Glands in flowers secrete the sugary fluid bees gather and turn into honey.

clue.text: I'm with it on a hill says the mimic

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A mimic boasts of being trendy and on a hilltop.
explanation.walkthrough: A TOR is a rocky hilltop, common on Dartmoor in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A mimic copies others, just as one who imitates does.

parts.note: the final moments of a match, what commentators call the closing seconds before the whistle

explanation.surface: Broadcasters' cliché for the end of a game.
explanation.definitionFit: The closing moments before a deadline or the end of a game are known by this phrase.

parts.note: the London palace of the Archbishop of Canterbury gives its name to degrees the archbishop confers

explanation.surface: A grand academic honour.
explanation.walkthrough: The Archbishop of Canterbury's London residence is a palace, and the degrees he can award are named after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Degrees awarded by the Archbishop of Canterbury bear the name of his London palace.

clue.text: Not very striking but makes his mark

definitions.meaning: a strike-breaker, who works on while his fellows strike
a crust over a healing wound that leaves a mark

explanation.surface: A dull man who still manages to leave his mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not very striking' looks like 'unremarkable'; it means one who refuses to join a strike.
explanation.definitionFit: A strikebreaker is called by this insulting word, which is also the dry crust over a wound that may leave a mark.

clue.text: Inherently recollected in "I remember, I remember"

definitions.text: Inherently recollected in "I remember, I remember

parts.words: Inherently recollected in "I remember, I remember
parts.note: Thomas Hood's poem 'I remember, I remember' looks back on the poet's early years as a lad

explanation.surface: A poem of memory recalls something by its nature.
explanation.walkthrough: Hood's poem recalls the house where he was born and his youth; 'inherently' hints the word naturally lies within those memories.
explanation.definitionFit: The time of being a young lad is what Hood's poem looks back on.

definitions.note: a phrase describing where the noun is found

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
a nail fastens things together

explanation.surface: A silver clasp worn on the finger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silver fastener on one's finger' looks like a ring; the answer is a torn strip of skin by the fingernail.
explanation.definitionFit: A hangnail, the sore strip of torn skin beside a fingernail, goes by this older name.

indicators.note: the letters of the first two words are cast in a different form, rearranged into the old name

explanation.surface: A tourist begs to be followed around the old island.
explanation.walkthrough: TAIL ME rearranged gives the Roman name for the island of Malta, the place where St Paul was shipwrecked in Acts.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek and Latin name of the Mediterranean island was this, as in the account of St Paul's shipwreck.

parts.note: to let is to lease out
up means at an end, as in time's up

explanation.surface: Relief comes when a tenancy finishes.
explanation.definitionFit: A let-up is a pause or easing, a breather.

parts.note: one who passes off another writer's words as his own

explanation.definitionFit: An old word for one who steals another's writing and passes it off, related to plagiarism.

parts.note: the man a woman adores and idolises, the lead figure of romance

explanation.surface: The man a woman loves.
explanation.walkthrough: The Greek tale reverses it: the lady Hero was the one Leander loved, a second reading the clue leaves for the classical solver.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's idol, the man she admires, is her champion of romance.

clue.text: Having a right to distinction in the ultimate

indicators.note: in places the honour inside the word for the final point

parts.note: the ultimate is the end
a title is a distinction, such as a knighthood

explanation.surface: Claiming one deserves an honour at the very last.
explanation.definitionFit: To be entitled is to hold a claim or right to something.

clue.text: Where a coin's tossed, and lost perhaps

definitions.text: Where a coin's tossed, and lost perhaps

indicators.note: tossed, as when coins are thrown about, signals the letters being jumbled

explanation.surface: A gambling house where money is staked and often lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tossed' rearranges A COIN'S; the whole clue then describes the gaming house.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaming house is where money is wagered and frequently lost.

clue.text: Keats and Longfellow were both on a Derby winner

definitions.text: Keats and Longfellow were both on a Derby winner

parts.words: Keats and Longfellow were both on a Derby winner
parts.note: both poets wrote works with the same title, the name of a Titan, which was also borne by the 1933 Derby winner

explanation.surface: Two poets backed the same horse at Epsom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'were both on' looks like betting; it means each wrote a work of that title: Keats a poem, Longfellow a prose romance. The Derby, Britain's great flat race at Epsom, was won in 1933 by a horse of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of a Titan, the father of the sun god, was the title of works by both poets and of a famous racehorse.

parts.note: near means close
a copper is a penny, D in old British money (denarius)

explanation.surface: A suspect told to keep quiet with a policeman nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a policeman; it is a penny, D in pre-decimal British money.
explanation.definitionFit: Something shut up, as a shop is, is no longer open.
